---
title: "Exercises — RNA libraries"
---

Pen and paper. The problems follow the two decks: choosing a route, strandedness, small RNA,
and tag against full length.

# Part 1 — Choosing a route

## E1. A degraded tumour sample

You have total RNA from archived FFPE human tumour sections, with most molecules under 200 nt.
You want gene expression, including lncRNAs and histone genes.

a. Poly(A) selection or rRNA depletion?
b. What does the coverage along transcripts look like in each case?
c. Which primer would you use for the first strand, and why not the other?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Ask what each method needs the RNA to still have, and what is left on a fragment that has been cut.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. rRNA depletion. Cut RNA has lost its tail unless it is the 3' piece, so selection would keep
   only the 3' fragments. Histone mRNA and many lncRNAs have no tail at all.
b. Poly(A) selection gives a steep 3' bias. Depletion gives coverage along the whole transcript,
   though it is lower for long transcripts because short fragments do not span the sequence.
c. Random hexamers. Oligo-dT needs the tail and would reproduce the 3' bias that depletion is
   meant to avoid. Hexamers cost some composition bias at read starts and will prime on any
   remaining rRNA.
:::

## E2. A missing gene family

A poly(A)-selected library from human cells shows almost no reads on the replication-dependent
histone genes, yet a depleted library from the same cells does. Explain.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Replication-dependent histone mRNAs end in a stem-loop and carry no poly(A) tail. Oligo-dT beads
cannot hold them, so they are washed away with the rRNA. A depletion library keeps every RNA
except those with probe sites.
:::

## E3. Which depletion method

Your lab studies a human cell line and wants to remove rRNA, and also remove three abundant
mitochondrial-derived transcripts that take 15% of reads. Compare RNase H depletion, biotin
probes with beads, and Cas9 on cDNA, and say which property decides.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Think about what must be designed for a new target, and at what step the removal happens.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
All three need a sequence-specific reagent per target: DNA oligos, biotin probes, or guide RNAs.
The deciding property is how easily you can add targets and how early the removal acts. Adding
three more targets to an oligo or guide set is cheap in each case. Cas9 on cDNA acts last, on
the final adapter-flanked library, so it can remove targets that you only discover are abundant
after a first run. RNase H and probe methods act on RNA, before RT, so they also save the
reverse-transcription reagent that would otherwise be spent on the target.
:::

# Part 2 — Strand

## E4. Counting the damage

Two genes overlap by 2 kb on opposite strands. Gene A produces 800 read-pairs in the overlap
and gene B produces 200. An unstranded library is sequenced and reads in the overlap are
counted for any gene they fall on.

a. What counts do A and B get in the overlap?
b. How far off is each?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 1000 reads in the overlap, counted for both genes: A gets 1000 and B gets 1000.
b. A is 25% too high, since 1000 against 800. B is five times too high, since 1000 against 200.
   The weaker gene is hit hardest.
:::

## E5. Strandedness is 88%, not 99%

A dUTP library from human liver has 12% of reads on the wrong strand. List three possible causes
and say how you would tell them apart.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Each cause acts at a different step. Think of one in first strand, one in second strand and one
after ligation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
- The RT copied DNA: actinomycin D was left out or too dilute, giving antisense first strand.
  The wrong-strand reads scale with expression, so they are highest on abundant genes.
- dUTP was not incorporated in the second strand, for example because of dTTP carry-over. The
  U-marked strand is then amplified. The wrong-strand fraction would be uniform across all
  genes.
- The silencing step did not act: the polymerase read through, or USER did not cut. The same
  uniform signature as the previous cause; compare with an earlier lot or a different
  polymerase.
:::

## E6. The wrong polymerase

A colleague swaps the PCR polymerase in a dUTP protocol for one that copies through uracil,
because it is cheaper. The library yield is fine. What happens to the data?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Both strands now amplify, so half of the molecules come from the marked second strand. The
library is no longer stranded: half of the reads are on the wrong strand, and the antisense
signal in the previous exercise returns. Yield and quality metrics will look normal, which is
why this goes unnoticed. A strandedness check is the only way to see it.
:::

# Part 3 — Small RNA

## E7. Why pre-adenylated

You ligate a normal 5' phosphorylated DNA adapter to a miRNA with T4 RNA ligase 1 and ATP.
Describe the products, and say what the pre-adenylated, 3'-blocked adapter with a truncated
ligase changes.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
With ATP present, any 5' phosphate and 3' hydroxyl in the tube is a substrate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The ligase uses ATP to adenylate any 5' phosphate end. The miRNA has both a 5' phosphate and a
3' OH, so it can ligate to itself, forming circles and concatemers, and the adapter can ligate
to itself too. With a pre-adenylated adapter the activated end already exists and ATP is
omitted, so the truncated ligase cannot activate the miRNA's own 5' phosphate. The 3' block on
the adapter stops it from ligating to itself. The only joint that can form is miRNA 3' OH to
adapter 5' App.
:::

## E8. A dimer peak

The Bioanalyzer trace of your small-RNA library shows a large peak slightly below the miRNA
peak. You have very little RNA. Propose three changes, in order of how early they act, and
say what each one costs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
1. Reduce the adapter concentration in the ligation. Fewer leftovers form dimers, but ligation
   efficiency falls, which matters most when RNA is scarce.
2. Enzymatic removal of free 3' adapter before the second ligation, as in kits that include it.
   It costs a step, but acts before the dimer can form.
3. Size selection after PCR. It works on the product, so it always helps, but the dimer is only
   a few tens of bases shorter, so the gel must be high resolution and some product is lost.
:::

## E9. Footprints with the wrong ends

An RNase I digest leaves ribosome footprints with a 5' hydroxyl and a 3' phosphate. If you ligate
a pre-adenylated 3' linker directly, what happens, and what step would you add?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The ligase needs a 3' hydroxyl, and the footprint has a 3' phosphate, so almost nothing ligates
and the library is empty. Treating with T4 PNK, which removes the 3' phosphate, fixes this.
The 5' hydroxyl does not matter here, because the footprint's 5' end is never ligated: the RT
copies it, and the cDNA is circularised afterwards.
:::

# Part 4 — Tag against full length

## E10. Three questions, three routes

Pick one protocol and one reason for each:

a. Gene counts from 5000 single cells, lowest cost per cell.
b. Which isoform of one gene is expressed in 40 individual cells.
c. The exact transcription start sites in human liver.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. A 3' tag protocol with the barcode in the RT primer, such as CEL-Seq2: cells are pooled
   before amplification, so cost per cell is low, and one end is enough for counting.
b. A full-length protocol such as SMART-seq2: reads must cover the exons that distinguish the
   isoforms. 40 cells is few enough that the cost per cell is acceptable.
c. A cap-selected 5' protocol such as CAGE or STRT-seq. Cap selection ensures reads start at
   the true 5' end.
:::

## E11. Template switching is not a proof of full length

A SMART-seq2 library shows read starts spread across many internal positions of a gene. Your
collaborator concludes that there are many alternative promoters. What is the alternative
explanation, and what would you do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Which RNA molecules can receive the extra Cs?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The RT also adds extra Cs to any RNA end it reaches, including fragments of degraded RNA that
have no cap, so a TSO can attach there too. Internal starts may be degradation products rather
than promoters. Check RNA integrity, compare with a cap-selected dataset, or use a method that
selects through the cap, such as cap trapping, before calling start sites.
:::

## E12. How many cycles

You have 20 pg of cDNA from one cell and need about 2 ng before tagmentation. Assume the PCR
efficiency is 85% per cycle, so each cycle multiplies by 1.85.

a. How many cycles?
b. What goes wrong if you run five more?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. The fold needed is 2 ng over 20 pg, which is 100. Cycles = ln 100 divided by ln 1.85, which
   is 4.605 divided by 0.615, about 7.5, so 8 cycles. In practice the first cycles are less
   efficient and kits use more, so use the number the protocol gives and check the yield.
b. Extra cycles add little mass, since the reaction runs out of primers and enzyme. They do add
   more PCR duplicates, more bias against difficult templates, and more chimeric products
   between molecules. With no UMI there is no way to remove the duplicates later.
:::

# Self-check

1. Why does poly(A) selection give 3' bias on degraded RNA?
2. What does RNase H depletion need that a poly(A) selection does not?
3. What marks the second strand, and what is different between TruSeq and NEBNext in using it?
4. Which of the two ligases in a small-RNA protocol needs ATP, and why does the order matter?
5. Why is circularisation used in Ribo-seq?
6. What does a TSO contain, and what extra bases on the RNA does it pair with?
7. Which type of protocol would you choose for counting, and which for isoforms?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. Cutting removes the tail from all but the 3' piece, so only the 3' piece is kept.
2. A set of DNA oligos covering the rRNA of the species, plus RNase H and a DNase step.
3. dUTP in the second strand. TruSeq relies on a polymerase that stalls at dU; NEBNext uses USER enzyme to cut at dU.
4. T4 RNA ligase 1 with ATP, for the 5' adapter. The 3' adapter is pre-adenylated and uses no ATP. The order ensures that the 5' step acts only on molecules that already carry a 3' adapter.
5. It places the end that has no adapter next to the linker, so one primer pair amplifies across the junction without a second ligation.
6. A 5' blocker, a PCR handle, an optional barcode or UMI, and a 3' run of G; it pairs with the extra Cs added by the RT.
7. A 3' tag protocol for counting; a full-length protocol for isoforms.
:::
